title: Urinary Bladder Anatomy: Detrusor, Trigone & Sphincters
description: Learn urinary bladder anatomy behind the pubic symphysis, covering the transitional urothelium, three-layer detrusor muscle, smooth trigone, and sphincter.
h1: Urinary Bladder Anatomy: Detrusor Wall, Trigone and Sphincters
blurb: A compliant three-layered detrusor muscle reservoir lined by stretchable transitional urothelium, guarded by a smooth trigone and dual urethral sphincters.
lead: Resting on the pelvic floor just behind the pubic bones, the urinary bladder is a hollow muscular reservoir that expands smoothly as it fills and contracts on command. In this illustrated guide to urinary bladder anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including dome (apex), detrusor muscle, urothelium, trigone—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Resting on the pelvic floor just behind the pubic bones, the urinary bladder is a hollow muscular reservoir that expands smoothly as it fills and contracts on command. The bladder is a muscular sac lined by transitional (urothelial) epithelium that stretches from five cell layers down to two as it fills. The detrusor muscle contracts under parasympathetic control (S2–S4) while the internal sphincter (smooth muscle) and external sphincter (skeletal, pudendal nerve) keep urine in. The trigone — the triangle between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice — is smooth because it develops from the mesonephric duct, and its oblique ureteric tunnels act as flap valves preventing reflux. Micturition is a spinal reflex under voluntary control from the pons and cortex. Within the human body, the urinary bladder (Vesica urinaria) is situated in pelvis, behind the pubic symphysis, receives arterial perfusion via superior & inferior vesical arteries (internal iliac), and is innervated by parasympathetic S2–S4 (contracts) · sympathetic T11–L2 (stores).

The dome (apex) (Apex vesicae) is the superior part, pointing toward the pubic symphysis and connected to the urachus (median umbilical ligament). Physiologically, the dome (apex) expands upward into the abdomen as the bladder fills. The detrusor muscle (Musculus detrusor) is three layers of interlacing smooth muscle with the wall thickened into trabeculae when obstructed. Physiologically, the detrusor muscle governs contraction empties the bladder; relaxation allows storage at low pressure. The urothelium (Epithelium transitionale) is stratified transitional epithelium with umbrella cells whose plaques make it impermeable to urine. Physiologically, the urothelium governs a stretch-tolerant, urine-proof lining. The trigone (Trigonum vesicae) is the smooth triangle bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; mucosa firmly bound to muscle. Physiologically, the trigone governs funnel for emptying; its stretch receptors trigger the micturition reflex. Structurally, the ureteric orifices (Ostia ureterum) comprises slit-like openings of the ureters at the posterolateral corners of the trigone, with oblique intramural tunnels. Physiologically, the ureteric orifices governs one-way entry of urine; the tunnel acts as a flap valve. The internal urethral orifice (Ostium urethrae internum) is the inferior angle of the trigone where the bladder neck meets the urethra. Physiologically, the internal urethral orifice governs outlet guarded by the internal sphincter.

Clinically, regarding the dome (apex), a patent urachus can leak urine at the umbilicus in a newborn. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the detrusor muscle, chronic outlet obstruction (prostate) hypertrophies it into trabeculae and diverticula; overactivity causes urge incontinence. In clinical pathology involving the urothelium, its instability to carcinogens (smoking, aniline dyes) makes transitional-cell carcinoma the classic bladder cancer. Medical evaluation of the trigone also notes that the interureteric ridge between the orifices is the first landmark sought at cystoscopy.
